#1570. Juventus and Torino the only Serie A sides without a penalty either way after 11 rounds

Eleven rounds into the Serie A season, Juventus have neither won nor conceded a penalty, a distinction shared only with Torino. With the league's penalty rate down and the team seventh, the João Mario handball in Florence has become the clearest example of a call that went against them.

Juventus have reached the November break without a single penalty decision in their league matches. Seven sides are still waiting for a penalty in their favour: Roma, Juventus, Torino, Lecce, Fiorentina, Sassuolo and Udinese. Seven have yet to concede one: Inter, Milan, Como, Juventus, Napoli, Torino and Genoa. Only the two Turin clubs appear on both lists.

That makes Juventus an outlier, even in a season of fewer spot-kicks. Sportmediaset puts the number of teams still waiting for a penalty partly down to the new refereeing approach introduced by Orsato.

The wider numbers show a quieter season from the spot. The 24 penalties so far work out at about 0.22 per match, compared with 0.28 and 0.27 in the two previous seasons. The drop was sharpest early on. Only five of the 24 penalties came in the first five rounds.

The trend has not been flat since then. The rate rose to 0.31 per match after the September international break. Juventus have not shared in that rise. Their total in both columns remains zero.

The contrast with last season is clear. Juventus were awarded five league penalties then. They also had the last three saved: David’s against Lecce, Yildiz’s against Cremonese and Locatelli’s against Sassuolo.

The case that has drawn most attention came late in the 2-2 draw at Fiorentina. João Mario handled the ball. No penalty was given. Gianluca Rocchi, who now works as a DAZN pundit, said it should have been a spot-kick. His reasoning was that the arm was out wide and the player had time to move it, even though the ball came from a teammate.

Luciano Spalletti signalled that he also saw a penalty. He chose not to complain publicly about the decision.

Close calls carry weight at this stage. Juventus are seventh on 18 points, six behind fourth place. Champions League qualification is in doubt. An injury-hit squad cannot easily absorb lost points from decisions at the margins.

The run after the break will test whether the pattern holds. Venezia, the next league opponents, are among five clubs to have conceded three penalties, the league’s highest total. Frosinone, Bologna, Atalanta and Sassuolo share that figure. Sassuolo are also on the list of sides yet to be awarded one.

The schedule is crowded. After Venezia, Juventus host Omonia in the Europa League. A league trip to Como follows, then Sassuolo at home in the Coppa Italia. Como have yet to concede a penalty this season.

The first of those fixtures has already moved. Lega Serie A brought Juventus v Venezia forward to Sunday 22 November at 12:30, from its original slot on Monday 23 November at 20:45.

#1569. Enzo Maresca tinkers his way to nervy Man City win

Few in elite sport have the luxury of managing their own endings as Pep Guardiola did at Manchester City, yet no one can ever fully control a beginning. Enzo Maresca’s City started their Premier League season with a win, in the end, but three points masked the scale of the job he faces.

The narrative focus has been the impossibility of filling the personality void Guardiola leaves at a club sculpted in his image. That macro reading overlooks the number of distinct issues with City that Maresca must fix. A new midfield has to be recruited then blooded, a jittery defence needs settling down, and Phil Foden clearly requires help to recover the form which made him Premier League player of the year as recently as 2024.

All of that can wait after this victory against Bournemouth, which quietened some of the alarms from last weekend’s 3-0 defeat by Arsenal in Cardiff. Josko Gvardiol scored an injury-time winner after City had trailed for most of the match, much of it a sloppy slog for the home side, who went behind in the 26th minute. The introduction of Rayan Cherki for Nico O’Reilly revived some familiar attacking effusiveness.

A lesser-spotted VAR-aided double celebration capped a tense but ultimately joyful day for Maresca. Marc Guéhi equalised from Cherki’s well-taken corner in the final minutes, then the expanded Etihad Stadium rapturously celebrated Gvardiol’s apparent winner, only to see it flagged offside. Video assistant Paul Howard intervened to show Gvardiol was onside from Cherki’s pass, before City’s fans, players and staff shouted twice as loud for twice as long to salute a morale-boosting victory.

Joško Gvardiol scores in stoppage time! 👊 pic.twitter.com/FrTrfIg3ur

“It’s the perfect day to be honest,” Maresca said, although he may wish to set his expectations slightly higher. The East Stand which faces the dugouts at the Etihad unfurled a banner before the game welcoming him back to Manchester after his spell as Guardiola’s assistant. “I was very pleased when the game started, to watch the banner at the other side, and I was pleased at the end because we gave them the joy of the three points.”

His team made a fluid and furious start to Premier League football, suffused with a desire to prove the Community Shield is just a jumped-up friendly. A newly streamlined short-haired Erling Haaland ran with impatience, Elliot Anderson was a sinewy presence in midfield, Foden pulled off a gorgeous flick which led to a shot by Rico Lewis, well saved by Djordje Petrovic.

Maresca’s selection was surprising, with six defenders in his XI, some deployed unexpectedly. Guéhi partnered Anderson in defensive midfield, while their England team-mate O’Reilly was often just behind Haaland in a No 10 role. There was an air of destiny about one O’Reilly run down the left flank in the first half, cruising to the byline and crossing presentably. Haaland was well positioned in the middle, but utterly fluffed his lines. Samson similes on standby, although perhaps he too was short of full match fitness during his early-season visit from the Philistines?

Momentum shifted after Haaland’s miss, and Bournemouth took the lead when an innocuous high ball flummoxed Abdukodir Khusanov and Rúben Dias. They both pursued it, neither could make decisive contact and it left Evanilson on the ball with space to manufacture an unmissable cross for Marcus Tavernier.

Marcus Tavernier fires Bournemouth ahead against Manchester City! 💥 pic.twitter.com/lSyNRfrTlc

Marco Rose, their new manager, is facing a similarly daunting task to Maresca in living up to a predecessor who led Bournemouth to their highest-ever league finish and European football. “How the game went, it was quite unlucky to lose,” he said. “We had two situations, one corner kick and one attacking when we defended too passive, and that’s why we lost.”

His team showed an appealing coiled-spring quality after weathering the early City onslaught. They have players of class with the ever lively Tavernier, new signing António Silva seamlessly replacing Marcos Senesi at centre-back and silky Alex Scott, the Guernsey Grealish, whose current standing has now overtaken the man who gave him his nickname.

They could not hang on here though, with Guéhi atoning for a free header planted wide with his day-saving equaliser. Cherki’s corner was nodded in from around the six-yard line then, with the game in the balance, the Frenchman provided another, thanks in part to the semi-automated gods smiling on Gvardiol and his new manager.

"That is an EXTRAORDINARY miss!" 🫣Marc Guehi misses a golden opportunity to equalise for Manchester City! pic.twitter.com/Jl96MMmQeP

No mistakes this time from Marc Guehi 😤 pic.twitter.com/xlCJXWUzz6

City will need more, especially in midfield. Anderson at his best can cover the ground and roles of two men, which is just as well as City await reinforcements. The incoming Ayyoub Bouaddi will help, but it is a big ask for an 18-year-old to fill a spot vacated by a Ballon d’Or winner. Maresca was asked after the match about finding a “new Rodri” and deadpanned “Marc Guéhi”, who played acceptably, but is probably not a long-term solution.

There was a jadedness at times from City, which is not a great way to start the season, although they will surely improve with a bolstered squad and fitness levels. Maresca said “four or five” of his players who returned late from the World Cup are still effectively in pre-season training, including Haaland and Anderson.

Of course City are not the finished article, what team are one game into a new season? While there is a vast gap from this performance to their best, it was still impressive to smuggle three points from zero with six minutes left to play. Guardiola’s influence will be hard to shake, but that need not be a negative.

Marc Guéhi: Central Midfield Edition pic.twitter.com/ViBZqOroB2

The Maresca era begins with the most dramatic of wins. City were trailing 1-0 at 84 minutes, but somehow managed to turn it around.

Emery doesn’t hang around. I’m not convinced he shook Hurzeler’s hand.

Manchester City 2 Bournemouth 1 (Gvardiol) Oh my, Gvardiol has the ball in the back of the net but his “winner” is ruled out by the linesman instantly. Cherki had wriggled this way and that on the edge of the box before sliding in the Croatian who dispatched the ball with aplomb.

BUT, replays show that Hill’s back foot played Gvardiol onside ...so the late, late goal is GIVEN!

Maresca jumps for joy, the Etihad erupts. But that is heartbreaking for Bournemouth...

Joško Gvardiol scores in stoppage time! 👊 pic.twitter.com/FrTrfIg3ur

Guehi saves the day for City, scoring a harder header than the sitter he missed early in this half. Nice corner from Cherki was powererd in from close to the penalty spot. Crowd smells blood with five minutes left but Bournemouth look to still have a bit in the tank.

Incidentally, Jack Grealish is on for City with the ‘Guernsey Grealish’ Alex Scott still out there for Bournemouth, who is presumably worth about double in today’s transfer market? Can’t be often that a player shares pitch with his nickname-giver as their careers head in opposite direction. Wonder if Lionel Messi was ever described as “the new Roman Riquelme?” and played against him?

Bournemouth have responded well to getting pegged back, playing through City, who are desperate for a shot at three points. Gannon-Doak stands up a cross but finds the gloves of Donnarumma.

City attempt to break down the left but Grealish just runs out of road.

Manchester City 1 Bournemouth 1 (Guehi) He might have missed a sitter earlier on, but when presented with a similar opportunity from a corner - this time via Cherki from the right - Guehi makes no mistake, planting his header beyond Petrovic.

No mistakes this time from Marc Guehi 😤 pic.twitter.com/xlCJXWUzz6

Haaland threatens to break free down Bournemouth’s right but Truffert just about recovers and clears his lines.

Grealish replaces Foden, who slopes straight down the tunnel.

Jebbison calls Donnarumma - who has been a spectator for the past 20 minutes - into action with a sharp header. There is a delay in the taking of the subsequent corner as Adams and Jebbison jostle for position with the City goalkeeper, but it’s all for nothing as the delivery is dealt with.

Foden goes into the book for a foul on substitute Jebbison. A tad harsh, perhaps. Looks like he semi-slipped into that contact.

Ayari attempts an bicycle kick but cannot beat Bizot. That would have been a goal of the month contender had it found the back of the net.

Guehi combines with Foden down the right and hits the by-line before a digging out a cross to Haaland. The ball is behind him and his right-footed effort does not have the requisite power to beat Petrovic, who has been immense today.

Bit better from City, Foden curls just wide, Semenyo has a shot well saved by Petrovic. Meres presence of Cherki seems to have injected some urgency to their attacks and fear to Bournemouth’s defence. Not sure City look quite ready for this season. Obviously there will be further incomings but they are leggier and more haphazard than Bournemouth.

Chance! Foden, Nunes and Cherki work the ball from right to left on the edge of Bournemouth’s box, eventually falling to Haaland who scoops the ball over with his usually lethal left boot. The visitors had plenty of men between ball and goal and that caused the Norwegian to snatch at his effort.

Villa started last season with no win in their first five games and just three points. They then rallied strongly after that. This one feels different as the rebuild is so significant. Second half has been very flat so far.

City are asking questions now. Cherki combines with Foden down the right and the Englishman shifts the ball on to his favoured left boot and his curled effort deflects off Silva and out for a corner which comes to nothing.

Semenyo breaks free down the left channel and fires the ball across the keeper towards the far post, but Petrovic gets a strong hand to it and pulls off a good save.

Kostoulas thinks he’s made it five having followed in a fizzed-in Costinha effort that had struck the post. But the strike is scrubbed off immediately and replays back up the linesman’s decision.

Little sign of City finding the composure to take control of this match. Passing is getting ever-sloppier and Guehi put a free header painfully wide. Maresca’s team are dominating possession but would be no surprise if the next goal was another Bournemouth sucker-punch. Kovacic and Cherki about to come on, the latter should improve the picture.

Anderson receives treatment on the pitch and is subsequently replaced by Kovacic. The Englishman stretches out his right leg as he leaves the field of play and keeps it elevated as he takes his position on the bench.

Dunk creates some chaos in Villa’s box, spinning in a lofted through-ball which Bizot palms away under duress. Rutter then pulls an effort wide off the resulting corner.

Nunes makes an instant impact, beating Scott easily down the right before standing up a cross to the far post where Haaland is waiting. Two Bournemouth defenders mirror the forward’s leap and do enough to disrupt his flow - and Semenyo’s - the Ghanaian also misses the ball.

Shows how few options Emery has - he has not made a change at half-time. Villa have been a little brighter going forward. A good run from Hemmings to play in Maatsen, and then the Villa teenager misjudging a cross when McGinn put him in down the right. But Brighton will feel there are more goals for them.

Maresca looks to his bench and brings on Nunes for Lewis.

Brighton are still going for this. Gross’ corner from the left reaches Vuskovic at the back post, but he cannot poke the ball past Bizot.

You’ll do well to see a worse miss all season! Guehi is afforded the freedom of Manchester inside the box from an inswinging corner but he somehow glances the ball wide.

"That is an EXTRAORDINARY miss!" 🫣Marc Guehi misses a golden opportunity to equalise for Manchester City! pic.twitter.com/Jl96MMmQeP

De Cuyper tees up another corner from the right. His punched-in delivery picks out Ayari perfectly on the edge of the box but the Swede’s volley flies just wide. A touch ball to hit first time.

Villa have opted to sit in and hope they can see this out without further damage. The Sky Sports cameras pan to a now sparse away end where some are still cheering their side on. Fair play.

Play has resumed at the Etihad and immediately City begin circulating the ball in front of Bournemouth’s first line of pressure. It’s all very slow still and they are unable to penetrate their opponents’ robust mid-black.

Boos at half time as City leave the field, although will charitably assume they are more for referee Jared Gillet for his late non-award of a penalty. Rico Lewis went down in the box but it looked soft. Another early test for Maresca, Bournemouth are lively in attack and defending capably. City all pace and intent but not playing with much patience or finesse.

Pretty horrifying first half from Villa. It was a strange team to start with – factoring in the four big summer sales and then the two absentees, Watkins and Emi Martinez. But this has been even worse than expected. Many of the team has just crumbled under the first sign of pressure. Pau Torres has been terrible. Joao Gomes picked up a yellow and then a red card on his debut. Villa started with Buendia as a centre-forward and now - with ten men - are just trying to play without any striker at all. Emery’s options are limited. Funny to think they started really well and should have taken the lead through Buendia on five minutes.

There’s a shout for a penalty as Haaland knocks down a header at the back post for Lewis, who gets shoved to the ground clumsily by Scott. Nothing going though, and that’s the half.

There’s a coming together on the halfway line at the Etihad. Haaland and Silva tangle, which sets off a chain reaction as Kluivert comes steaming in, first towards Haaland and then Guehi. Evanilson is next on the scene and he gets a firm shove off Gvardiol.

City now looking shaky at the back. Cross-field balls in their half zipping past half a dozen in sky blue without intervention, shots from range going just wide, Donnarumma needing to save well to prevent a second.

Has stopped clicking up front as well, something isn’t going to plan when you have Haaland in your team but most of the high balls are heading towards Foden and O’Reilly.

CARTÃO VERMELHO! Gomes is sent off. Disaster for Villa. It was a kick at Rutter borne of frustration. McGinn was already walking Gomes away from referee Peter Bankes before the decision came. A clear kick to the chest after Rutter knocked him over. Gomes has been nowhere near the level required. He will never forget his Villa debut.

Ooof, Tavernier goes close with a lovely curled effort from 25 yards out. Just wide, however.

Kluivert gets a sight at goal moments later but is denied by Donnarumma who gets down to his left sharply to keep the ball out.

Haaland looks to breathe life into City’s rather drab performance by chasing down Petrovic.

Moments later, he directs a glancing header towards goal and forces the Bournemouth keeper into a smart stop. Foden’s subsequent corner is not up to much.

VAR is looking at an incident on the halfway line. Rutter barges into Gomes and the midfielder kicks out at the Brighton front man. The referee is sent to the screen and a red card correctly follows. A dreadful performance from Gomes.

Villa have really struggled under pressure at the back. Going forward they still look have enough creative players that they are not embarrassed. But Brighton are dominating them with the press in the Villa half. There are not many options for Emery to change at half-time. Mings? Garnacho?

Some very untidy defending for the opening goal here which comes against the run of play, if not drastically so. Khusanov was bamboozled by an  innocuous high ball, couldn’t make decisive contact and left space for it to reach Evanlison on the right, whose cross was hard for Tavernier to miss.

A few groans and grumbles already from the home fans, Guehi getting some flak for squandering a decent position near the Bournemouth area and giving away the ball. Not really his job to be on the ball and making stuff happen near the opposition box though, is it?

This is looking very bad for Villa. Two Brighton goals in one minute for Jack Hinshelwood and it is 4-0 with 31 mins played. The first was a very well-worked goal – Ayari cross nodded down by Gomez for Hinshelwood to head in. The second was just another mistake by Villa – Ayari stealing the ball from Joao Gomes to create a critical turnover. Villa started well but they look completely outgunned physically. Brighton are really pressing home their advantage in the duels. Lots of pressure on the likes of young George Hemmings and Gomes.

"Absolutely INCREDIBLE!"Jack Hinshelwood scores two in a matter of minutes and Brighton are ripping Aston Villa apart! 🤯 pic.twitter.com/tvS5qMJJ8C

Brighton 4 Aston Villa 0 (Hinshelwood) That’s two in a matter of seconds. Again, Villa try to play out from the back and again they get caught out. Ayari telescopes in a leg to take the ball away from Gomes on the edge of Villa’s box and Hinshelwood is there to tuck it home.

Brighton 3 Aston Villa 0 (Hinshelwood) A cross from the left is nodded back across goal by Gomez and Hinshelwood is there to finish.

Manchester City 0 Bournemouth 1 (Tavernier) Bournemouth carve City open with ease. A long ball from Smith is not dealt with and Rayan works the ball out to Evanilson who needs just a brief look up before picking out Tavernier, who finishes at the back post.

Marcus Tavernier fires Bournemouth ahead against Manchester City! 💥 pic.twitter.com/lSyNRfrTlc

City have not yet reached the intensity levels they usually show when in full swing. Semenyo tries to inject some energy with a burst down the left but Rayan does well to track back and cut it out.

Villa’s defence is floundering. This time a corner delivered from the right sails over everyone, including Bizot, but the back-post nod-down evades everyone and Villa clear their lines.

Bright start from City, but momentum has diminished since an odd miss from Haaland, whose limbs looked unusually muddled after O’Reilly soared down the left wing and crossed presentably. Move had an air of inevitability to it, was unexpected not to see the Norwegian score. Prepare the Samson similes.

The second goal from Brighton, and it’s direct. Georginio Rutter played through with a very straight ball, and Rutter had Pau Torres on the proverbial toast. De Cuyper kept up with his team-mate and ran onto the cross. Villa have not been bad. Torres, however, is having a dreadful afternoon.

Brighton 2 Aston Villa 0 (De Cuyper) Rutter does brilliantly to latch on to a ball over the top from well inside his half. He bursts down the left channel before lashing a fierce ball across the face of goal which De Cuyper turns in. Villa in all sorts of problems here.

What a start for Brighton!Maxim De Cuyper doubles their advantage! 🔵 pic.twitter.com/3WbyZlEhMV

Chance! O’Reilly bursts past Smith out on the left and picks out Haaland, who appears to be in two minds as to whether he wants to head or volley the ball. Instead he does neither and the chance goes begging.

Gomes leaves one on Ayari, which is risky given he has already picked up a booking. A red card at this point would be hugely damaging.

Brighton take the lead with an own goal from Victor Lindelof. An unfortunate one for the Swede who was trying to get Maxim De Cuyper’s shot off the line. It hit the post and ricocheted in off Lindelof. The fault lay with Pau Torres who gave the ball away needlessly. Very good turn from De Cuyper to make the room for the shot. Up until then, Villa - even with this unusual understrength side - were much the better.

Lewis is in fact playing right-back, with Guehi into defensive midfield alongside Anderson. O’Reilly advanced of both, with Gvardiol at left-back. All quite fluid, though, as you would expect from modern City.

Brighton 1 Aston Villa 0 (OG Lindelof) A disaster at the back for Villa. Pau Torres looks to play out from near the by-line but instead picks out De Cuyper inside Villa’s box. The wide man does well to steady himself before getting a shot away, which ricochets off the post, back on to Lindelof and into the net.

City have started brightly. Here Haaland slips in Lewis, who is unmissable with his new bleached hair, but Petrovic pulls off a smart save.

Chance! Ayari gets his pocket picked inside his own half by a buzzing Barkley. Buendia has a sight of goal but he slides the ball inches wide.

He’s at it again moments later, but he sends a third effort at goal over the bar.

Villa have started the brighter of the two sides. McGinn spins a deep free-kick into the box, which is cleared out to Buendia on the edge of the box but his shot sails over.

A warm minute’s applause for the former Manchester City manager.

Brighton are in their customary blue and white home kits shooting left to right, with Villa in black.

That’s a “Welcome Back Enzo” banner slowly cascading down the East stand. Feel that the tifo department has missed a trick, because it would have been very amusing to use a picture of Pep Guardiola, and see if anyone noticed. That could actually be Guardiola for all I know, my facial recognition is dreadful. Getting all of the trite “don’t they look similar!” observations out of my system ahead of the September cut-off point.

The teams have emerged from the tunnel at the Amex and the Etihad...

When asked by Sky Sports whether Ollie Watkins’ omission from the match-day squad was a sign that his Villa career was over, Emery pursed his lips and stared back at the reporter for a few seconds before saying: “Silence.”

After being pressed on the subject, he added: “No, no, no. We are playing today here. It’s OK. We are not speaking about [Ollie].”

"Silence" 🤫An unusual response from Unai Emery 😅 pic.twitter.com/kWNZtQu3PA

On taking charge of his first match as City head coach, Enzo Maresca told Sky Sports: “It’s big emotion. It’s a very nice feeling, the first game at home in front of our fans, so hopefully we can give them the three points.”

When asked about Elliot Anderson and the void left by Rodri, he added: “I think Elliot [Anderson] has to be himself; a good player, he’s going to be even better, but he has to be himself. Again, for me, there are no players that they are the same player, they are all different.

“We are happy with Elliot, but for sure, as we know, Rodri is a big player but he’s already gone. So now the focus is on the ones that are here with us and the ones that will probably arrive.”

Subs Steele, Strujik, Costinha, Svoboda, Osman, Yalcouye, David, Kostoulas, Yohanna

Aston Villa Bizot; Cash, Torres, Lindelof, Maatsen; Barkley, Kamara; McGinn, Gomes, Hemmings; Buendia

Manchester City Donnarumma; Khusanov, Dias, Guehi, Gvardiol; Anderson, Lewis; Semenyo, Foden, O’Reilly; Haaland

Bournemouth Petrovic; Smith, Silva, Hill, Truffert; Cook, Scott; Rayan, Kluivert, Tavernier; Evanilson

Brighton have spent around £100m this summer but of those only the Croatian centre-back, Luka Vušković, is in the starting XI to face Aston Villa. He cost £46m from Spurs. Brighton have, as ever, sold players with Jan-Paul Van Hecke the biggest price. The expectation is that Carlos Baleba will leave for Manchester United. He is not in the squad. The injured Yankuba Minteh would not have been involved today - but he is another likely departure. Player of the year Ferdi Kadioglu is missing with injury.

Pep Guardiola’s successor assessed the breadth of the challenge before him and offered a candid appraisal of how to replace the irreplaceable. “It would be silly to try and change it,” he said of Guardiola’s grand design.

Tito Vilanova was addressing the world’s media in Camp Nou. For Barcelona in 2012, read Manchester in 2026. Enzo Maresca would be wise to study the manual for standing on the shoulder of a giant.

Charged with maintaining the standards of a two-time Champions League-winning team many still consider the best ever, Vilanova’s big idea was effectively to leave the existing one alone, mastering the art of the subtle tweak.

Describing the transition as seamless barely does justice to the changeover; Vilanova’s Barcelona side won 23 of their first 25 La Liga matches, snatching back the title lost to Real Madrid in Guardiola’s farewell campaign. Tragically, the promise of further honours to build on sturdy foundations was realised by others as Vilanova died from cancer in 2014.

After a brief stint by Gerardo Martino, Luis Enrique gave the dream team of Lionel Messi, Andrés Iniesta and Sergio Busquets further La Liga titles and another Champions League win.

The so-called “impossible job” of being bound by the weight of the preceding genius, therefore, was no such thing.

The Villa team is missing six of the players who started the Europa League final against Freiburg on May 20. Four of them have left (Ezri Konsa, Morgan Rogers, Lucas Digne, Youri Tielemans) and Emi Martinez and Ollie Watkins might be leaving too - they are absent today. Belgian goalkeeper Marco Bizot starts and there is also a place for teenager George Hemmings. Emi Buendia in what looks like the central striker role. It is certainly a bracing opening day to the season for Unai Emery.

No sign of Watkins in what is an objectively underpowered Aston Villa line-up. There’s also no start for new signing Suzuki, with Emery preferring Bizot between the sticks. Academy graduate Hemmings makes his first Premier League start.

Representing Aston Villa 👊 pic.twitter.com/JjqgYhBzwb

TEAM NEWS! 🚨 Here's how we start 🆚 Villa! 👊 pic.twitter.com/nnFj5swsdg

Some eyebrows raised at the inclusion of Rico Lewis in City’s starting XI, presumably as a defensive midfielder given the presence of Dias, Guehi, O’Reilly and Khusanov on the team-sheet. He did not have a pleasant afternoon in Cardiff last weekend, although that could be said for several City players. Some lingering doubts about his physicality, in a Premier League becoming ever more hands-on, but Enzo Maresca knows him from his time as an assistant here and clearly rates him. Wonder whether that sentiment will endure if (when) City buy some new midfielders in the coming weeks.

🔵 TEAM NEWS🍒The first #afcb team of the new Premier League season 👊 pic.twitter.com/uJhTI01Jld

Haaland will make his 200th appearance for City this afternoon. Either Lewis or O’Reilly could be deployed alongside Anderson in central midfield.

Our first XI of the season! 🩵XI | Donnarumma, Khusanov, Dias (C), Guéhi, Gvardiol, Lewis, Anderson, O'Reilly, Semenyo, Foden, HaalandSUBS | Rulli, Marmoush, Kovačić, Cherki, Nico, Grealish, Aït-Nouri, Reis, Nunes🤝 @etihad pic.twitter.com/6wSBoP8jon

Welcome to live coverage of Sunday afternoon’s 2pm Premier League kick-offs. Enzo Maresca faces the unenviable task of following Pep Guardiola’s decade of dominance at Manchester City and his reign begins in earnest with a visit from Bournemouth, who themselves are ushering in a new era after Marco Rose succeeded Andoni Iraola. A bruising 3-0 defeat in the Community Shield last weekend does not bode well for City’s hopes of closing the gap to Arsenal, but Maresca will be telling his charges that this afternoon is a fresh start: a new week and a new competition, plus Erling Haaland has a new haircut…

The Italian’s squad has been shorn of World Cup winner Rodri, who departed for Barcelona this week, and the spotlight will turn to £116m club-record signing Elliot Anderson who is expected to make his Premier League debut with City. Jérémy Doku is out for two to three weeks after suffering a calf injury, which could open the door for Jack Grealish, with City bereft of wide options. City will have their work cut out as Bournemouth, fresh off a historic sixth-place finish last season, look to extend their 18-match unbeaten run from the end of last season. The Cherries won three of their five pre-season matches, which included an eye-catching 10-1 victory over Serie A side Genoa.

Brighton and Hove Albion welcome Aston Villa to the Amex for their 2026-27 season opener having travelled 220 miles north of the Arctic Circle to play Norwegian side Tromso in their Europa Conference league play-off on Thursday. Fabian Hurzeler’s side face the defending Europa League champions without Carlos Baleba, who is on the brink of joining Manchester United, as well as injured wingers Kaoru Mitoma and Yankuba Minteh. While Unai Emery has lost key players in Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans, Ezri Konsa and Lucas Digne, the funds raised has gone towards seven signings, with Zion Suzuki, the Japan goalkeeper, in line to make his first start for Villa.

#1568. Romano: Balde expected to leave Barcelona – Milan’s position after summer talks

AC Milan have been linked with a move for Alejandro Balde, but Fabrizio Romano claims some flexibility is needed from Barcelona.

In the past couple of weeks there has been more talk about Milan strengthening in the left-back role. Pervis Estupinan has not been convincing since his arrival, while Davide Bartesaghi and Diego Moreira have been used further forward in recent weeks.

Yunus Musah was even adapted to playing as a left-sided defender in the recent win over Genoa, so it’s clear that Ruben Amorim might welcome a more natural player for the role, one that fits his ideas of how to play.

In a video on his YouTube channel, Fabrizio Romano touched upon a number of different topics connected to Milan, from Francesco Camarda’s fate to the possibility of a young midfielder arriving. He also spoke about Balde – another recent link – and his words are via MilanNews.

“Balde is a name that can be a key player in January. Then, to be completely honest, he’s a foreign transfer name, being realistic. He earns more than €5 million net per season,” he began.

“Barcelona were willing to let him go in the summer, but wanted a permanent deal worth €50-55 million. As for Italy, despite Mendes also trying to see if there was any room for negotiation with Milan, there were never any real negotiations. Also because the costs are decidedly high.

“Balde still isn’t playing and will speak with Mendes today, who is on a mission to Barcelona to meet with the player and his family and figure out what to do in the January transfer window.

“I’d keep an eye on the possibility if the formula were to change, because these are currently foreign figures. But he’s a player to keep an eye on. We’ll see if he goes to Italy or abroad.”

#1567. SCOTLAND 2 NORTH MACEDONIA 1: John McGinn at the double to spare the blushes of Pocognoli's shaky Scots on skipper Robertson's big night

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:01 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 17:11 EST, 13 November 2026

On the night when the nation looked over its shoulder and celebrated the past, the here and now for Scotland looked distinctly uncertain.

Coming 40 years and a day after his friend, Sir Kenny Dalglish, pulled on a Scotland jersey for the 102nd and final time, Andy Robertson joined the great man on a mark which, for years, seemed beyond the reach of mere mortals.

By time up, history had mercifully repeated itself at Hampden. Back in the day, Dalglish, by then player-manager at Anfield, sailed into the international sunset on the back of a routine 3-0 win over Luxembourg.

Facing another opponent of modest ability, Robertson’s red letter day didn’t go quite as smoothly. Yet, when the Tottenham man is old and grey and reflecting on the night he created history, the annals will at least record a slender victory.

While his side did just about enough to prevail here, this was another fraught night for Sebastien Pocognoli.

You can talk about the need for patience under the new manager until the cows come home. But North Macedonia are 71st in FIFA’s rankings. Scotland are 43rd.

John McGinn celebrates in trademark fashion after netting Scotland's winner from the spot

At Hampden Park, in front of an expectant crowd, Scotland should be putting them to the sword with something to spare.

Yet, for long enough, the Belgian’s new-look side were flat, predictable and plodding. It said much that it took the intervention of VAR for them to get the penalty which would ultimately lead to three points being accrued.

John McGinn’s second half double saved the Belgian’s blushes and truthfully there was little else to get the Tartan Army off their seats.

Too many big-name players scarcely merited pass marks. Too few looked comfortable in the system the manager is trying to bed in.

If it was a step in the right direction, it was a small one. After five games under the affable Belgian, the progress has certainly not been startling.

While it goes without saying that beating the Swiss in St Gallen on Monday will be an inordinately tougher task, having some hope of moving up a place and securing a kinder draw for the Euros is still better than no hope.

Regardless of what pot they end up in when the draw is made in Belfast next month, a radical improvement will certainly be required across the board if they are to stand any chance of qualifying for the tournament via the front door.

As well as the achievements of Robertson and Dalglish, the career of Craig Gordon was acknowledged before the match with the 84-times capped keeper deservedly afforded a warm hand by the Tartan Army.

McGinn slots home his penalty after Ben Gannon-Doak had been brought down in the area

There were absolutely no excuses for Scotland here. North Macedonia were a tier-two team in name only. They arrived at Hampden having not won in 12 matches and not scored in eight.

Another Pocognoli game saw another back-three combination. This time Luke Graham was selected in the centre of the unit with Ryan Porteous and Kieran Tierney deployed either side of the Stoke man in what were their first appearances under the Belgian.

Robertson and Ben Gannon-Doak were tasked with providing the width in the 3-4-3. Scott McTominay slotted back into an advanced role beside John McGinn with the returning Che Adams asked to lead the line.

For all there was a healthy crowd in excess of 40,000 inside Hampden, the atmosphere was subdued. In the four Nations League games to date under the new manager, the side hadn’t exactly given the supporters much to feed off.

Despite some big guns returning, Scotland made a laboured start to their night’s work. It said much that Graham, on his second appearance, was busier than any defender in white.

The first opening came as a result of an opposition error. John McGinn found Billy Gilmour who fed the overlapping Robertson. The skipper’s cross was well out of Adams’ reach.

Sebastien Pocognoli got his first Hampden win as Scotland boss but it was a nervy night

Although Ljupche Doriev worried Angus Gunn with a curling effort, Scotland began to exert some degree of control on the match. Lewis Ferguson kept the visitors hemmed in with a header into McTominay’s feet. The Napoli man saw his shot on the spin well saved by Stole Dimitrievski.

Pocognoli was frustrated when Slovakian referee Michal Ocenas blew for a foul on McTominay, his justifiable gripe being that playing an advantage would have seen Robertson have a crack at goal.

Dimitrievski had a decent night. Although Adams’ flashing header from McGinn’s corner took a deflection, a reflex save at his near post added to Scotland’s frustration.

North Macedonia were a spirited but ordinary side. They still had enough to thwart Pocognoli’s men.

Gannon-Doak saw plenty of the ball down the right, yet the end product often wasn’t there. The Bournemouth man did tee up Billy Gilmour for one dangerous cross. McTominay tried to replicate his iconic overhead kick against Denmark nearly a year ago. This time, his aim wasn’t true.

You could hardly blame Pocognoli’s star man for failing to find the net on that occasion.

Scott McTominay attempts an overhead spectacular a year on from THAT goal at Hampden

That wasn’t the case a few moments later when Adams slipped him in. Dimitrievski saved McTominay’s strike with an outstretched leg when he should have been picking the ball out of his net.

Adams had just blazed a strike high over the top while one-on-one with the keeper although the offside flag saved his blushes.

The visitors came closer to edging ahead when Eljif Elmas played the pass of the match over Scotland’s static defence to pick out Ezgjan Alioski. His lay-off was smashed into the side net by Enis Bardhi.

A wholly uninspiring first-half concluded with Robertson advancing up the left and launching a cross halfway to Castlemilk. This was not going well.

Pocognoli waited on the edge of the pitch for his players returning, his enthusiastic applause clearly audible in the arena.

His hopes of a breakthrough at the outset of the second period were dashed in extraordinary fashion. Adams did well to chase a ball down to the line and cut it back. McTominay and his marker couldn’t connect, leaving Gilmour the simple task of firing into an unguarded net. Leaning back, his failure to even hit the target was unfathomable.

Elmin Rastoder celebrates after silencing Hampden with a leveller for North Macedonia

Within seconds, the sense of relief inside Hampden was palpable as the opener finally arrived. Porteous got enough distance on his clearing header for Adams to barge Visar Musliu out of the way.

McGinn was alert to the situation and burst into the box. His crisp strike finally had the beating of the goalkeeper.

It should have settled Pocognoli’s side and paved the way for a comfortable result. Instead, they were pegged back within three minutes.

It was all just so simple and so avoidable. Bardhi’s whipped corner only needed McTominay to outjump his man. Flat-footed as the delivery arrived, he could only watch on in horror as Elmin Rastoder’s flashing header beat Angus Gunn.

Although Gilmour worked the keeper with a low strike, North Macedonia also sniffed a second goal. Time and time again, they got into pockets of space on the flanks and fired in dangerous crosses.

Adams made way for Oli McBurnie, the Hull man desperately hoping for his first goal on his 21st international appearance. He had a gilt-edged chance to get off the mark when rolled in by McGinn, but selflessly passed to the overlapping Gannon-Doak.

Scotland move on to their final game away in Switzerland as they look to finish on a high note

The winger appeared to take a heavy touch which allowed the keeper to rescue the situation. VAR, however, spotted that Dimitrievski had impeded him. Penalty.

McGinn did the necessary from 12 yards, smashing the ball straight down the middle for his 24th international goal.

North Macedonia, to their credit, kept going for it. They sensed a fragility in Scotland. Everyone in the ground could.

McGinn’s calm conversion proved to be just about enough to get the job done. But it’s fair to suggest that we are still awaiting lift-off in the new era.

SCOTLAND (3-4-1-2): Gunn; Porteous, Graham, Tierney; Gannon-Doak (Hickey 76), Ferguson, Gilmour (Christie 76), Robertson; McGinn; Adams (McBurnie 67), McTominay. Booked: Ferguson. Manager: Sebastien Pocognoli.

NORTH MACEDONIA (4-2-3-1): Dimitrievski; Ilievski, Mladenovski, Musliu, Alioski; Gashtarov (Elezi 64), Elmas (Stankovski 78); Churlinov (Maleski 64), Bardhi, Doriev (Nikolov 85); Rastoder. Booked: None. Manager: Goce Sedloski.

#1566. Zhegrova plays 82 minutes in Kosovo’s 0-0 with Israel before Dublin decider for second

With Edon Zhegrova in the starting line-up, ten-man Kosovo held Israel to a goalless draw, a result that leaves them second in Nations League Group B3. The run-out gives a Juventus forward who rarely starts for his club valuable match fitness while Pierre Kalulu is injured.

In Pristina, the Juventus forward Edon Zhegrova was Kosovo’s main attacker against Israel.

Zhegrova tested Israel’s defence a couple of times in the first half but faded after the break, according to TuttoJuve. Dion Kacuri came on in his place.

Below Kosovo, Ireland have 5 points and Israel 3. Austria beat the Republic of Ireland 1-0 on the same Saturday.

Kosovo’s campaign has been uneven. They opened by beating the Republic of Ireland 1-0 on 24 September. Three days later they lost 3-1 away to Austria on 27 September. On matchday 3, they had also drawn 0-0 with Israel.

The final round pairs the Republic of Ireland with Kosovo and Israel with Austria. That leaves Ireland, sitting just below Kosovo, hosting the side directly above them. Zhegrova is set to be central to Kosovo’s hopes of holding on to second place.

For Juventus, the significance lies in the minutes. Zhegrova has started only once since joining the club. He sits low in Spalletti’s pecking order and has mostly featured in short spells off the bench.

More than 80 minutes as Kosovo’s focal point gives him match fitness. That could prove useful before Juventus face Venezia in Serie A and Omonia in the Europa League.

The squad is stretched. Scans at J|medical on 9 November found a low-grade injury to Pierre Kalulu’s left biceps femoris. The defender had felt muscle discomfort in his left thigh after the draw at Fiorentina. France withdrew him from their squad. The midfield is also short of bodies.

Spalletti has made clear he sees potential in the winger. “Edon se si completa un po’ può diventare un crack,” the coach said. If Edon rounds out his game a little, he can become a star.

We draw 0–0 with Kosovo in the UEFA Nations League. pic.twitter.com/SSS4UTPpw4

— ISRAEL FA (@ISRAELFA) November 14, 2026

Other clubs are paying attention too. Near the end of the summer window, Al-Ittihad made a move for the winger, and Monaco are also interested, Eurosport Italia reported. A strong finish to the international window would do his standing no harm, in Turin or elsewhere.

First comes Dublin. Kick-off at the Aviva Stadium is at 7.45pm UK time, with second place in the group at stake.

#1565. Çelik pulled from Türkiye XI with left hamstring tightness as Kalulu is already out

Zeki Çelik was withdrawn from Türkiye's starting line-up in Bordeaux after feeling tightness in the same left thigh muscle he injured in October. With Pierre Kalulu already sidelined, Juventus face tests that could leave them without both main right-sided defenders for Venezia and Omonia.

Zeki Çelik’s international week ended before kick-off in Bordeaux. The Juventus full-back was named in Türkiye’s starting line-up for Sunday’s Nations League match against France. His left hamstring tightened up as he went through the warm-up. He was taken out of the matchday squad as a precaution. Barış Alper Yılmaz started in his place.

An Emirhan Topçu own goal and a goal from Eli Junior Kroupi put France ahead. Abdülkerim Bardakcı scored a late reply for Türkiye. The result left France top of Nations League Group A1 with 13 points. They are through to the quarter-finals, which are due next March.

Çelik now returns to Turin for tests at J|Medical. Those results will decide how Juventus line up at the back after the international break.

The location is what worries Juventus. Çelik was substituted at half-time in the 2-2 Europa League draw with Rennes. His scans took place on the morning of Friday 23 October. He began a rehabilitation programme straight away and was expected back after the November break.

Tuttosport counted him among Spalletti’s first returning players, alongside Vicario and Gatti. The paper placed the Bordeaux problem in the biceps femoris of his left thigh. That is the same area as the October injury.

Çelik had only just returned after weeks out. That is why the warm-up incident has raised fears of a relapse. No diagnosis has yet been confirmed.

Juventus were already without Pierre Kalulu. He picked up the injury in the game against Fiorentina. He began treatment and was withdrawn from the France squad. Sky Sport Italia expected him to be out for about three weeks. That would rule him out of both the Venezia and Omonia matches.

If Çelik’s problem proves to be a relapse, Spalletti could be without both of his main right-sided defenders for those two games. The schedule offers little room for recovery. The Omonia match is the second of four games in 12 days.

The league position adds pressure. After 11 rounds Juventus are seventh in Serie A with 18 points. Their record reads five wins, three draws and three defeats.

Venezia visit Turin first, at 12:30 on 22 November in round 12 of Serie A. Omonia then come to the Allianz Stadium at 21:00 on 26 November in the Europa League league phase.

#1563. UNC13A splice correction rescues synaptic dysfunction induced by TDP-43 loss

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

TDP-43 nuclear depletion is a defining pathological feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia that induces widespread cryptic splicing defects in hundreds of transcripts1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8. Despite this, whether TDP-43 loss affects synaptic function has remained unclear. Here we show that TDP-43 loss induces a predegenerative state in which neurons remain structurally intact but suffer a substantial breakdown in synaptic communication. Genetic correction of a single cryptic splicing event in UNC13A was sufficient to rescue these deficits. We developed splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides that correct UNC13A cryptic splicing in human cortical and spinal motor neurons and in a humanized mouse model. In human neurons this intervention restored spontaneous and evoked synaptic vesicle release, release probability at individual synapses and wider network synchrony. Together, this establishes UNC13A splice correction as a mechanistically defined and genetically validated therapeutic strategy relevant to roughly 97% of patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and roughly 50% of patients with frontotemporal dementia with TDP-43 pathology.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a rapidly progressive and fatal neurodegenerative condition. Recently, antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting SOD1 and FUS have shown early promise in clinical trials9,10, but these approaches only benefit patients with SOD1 and FUS mutations—less than 3% of patients with ALS—leaving an urgent need for therapies for the remaining roughly 97% of patients with ALS. A common feature of all non-FUS and non-SOD1 ALS is the aggregation of TAR DNA binding protein-43 (TDP-43) in neurons1,2, a finding also observed in roughly 50% of both frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and Alzheimer’s disease2,11. However, no therapies that directly target TDP-43 are available, leaving the underlying nuclear loss of function (LoF) unaddressed. TDP-43 is an RNA-binding protein that is normally located in the nucleus and has crucial roles in the regulation of RNA splicing12,13. Cytoplasmic mislocalization of TDP-43 induces a nuclear LoF resulting in cryptic exon inclusion, cryptic alternative polyadenylation and/or exon skipping in some mature messenger RNA (mRNA) transcripts3. These events occur in hundreds of transcripts, including genes with crucial neuronal functions, such as STMN2, UNC13A and KCNQ2 (refs. 4,5,6,7,8). Whereas the impact of STMN2 mis-splicing on axonal regeneration and KCNQ2 exon skipping on intrinsic excitability has been studied, the direct impact of TDP-43 LoF on synaptic function has not been addressed.

Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have shown that single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) located within and proximal to a cryptic exon in UNC13A increase the risk of developing ALS and accelerate disease progression14,15,16. Under normal physiological conditions, these risk SNPs do not induce inclusion of the UNC13A cryptic exon, but after TDP-43 LoF, risk SNPs exacerbate cryptic exon inclusion leading to increased loss of functional RNA transcripts and protein6,7. UNC13A is a presynaptic protein that is required at the active zone to properly dock and prime synaptic vesicles for fusion with the plasma membrane17. Genetic deletion of Unc13a in mice leads to a roughly 90% reduction in spontaneous and evoked glutamatergic excitatory synaptic transmission18,19,20. Although the UNC13A genetic association strongly implicates this event in ALS pathogenesis, the contribution of TDP-43 LoF to synaptic dysfunction and the role of UNC13A cryptic splicing—particularly in the context of many mis-splicing events in other synaptic transcripts—is unaddressed. Resolving these outstanding questions is crucial for establishing whether correcting UNC13A splicing represents a viable therapeutic approach for restoring normal neuronal function.

Here we report that TDP-43 loss in mature human induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell-derived neurons induces loss of presynaptic UNC13A and a notable reduction in AMPA (α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazole propionic acid) receptor-mediated synaptic transmission, leading to a loss of coordinated network activity. Despite the widespread roles of TDP-43 in RNA regulation, isolated genomic deletion of the UNC13A cryptic exon rescues these deficits, demonstrating that this single event is a key driver of synapse dysfunction in ALS. To this end, we developed splice-switching ASOs that can rescue UNC13A mRNA splicing, UNC13A protein levels and UNC13A presynaptic localization, and restore both spontaneous and evoked synaptic transmission. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ASO treatment rescues UNC13A cryptic exon inclusion in a humanized mouse model that recreates this human-specific mis-splicing event. Thus, ASOs targeting the UNC13A cryptic exon represent an innovative therapeutic strategy for treating ALS and FTD, and their use for treating sporadic ALS is supported by genetic evidence.

TDP-43 plays important roles in development and therefore, to avoid interfering with neuronal maturation by depleting TDP-43 from the iPS cell stage, we used CRISPR–Cas12 gene editing to generate a cell line in which both endogenous copies of TDP-43 harbour a HaloTag to allow for proteolysis targeting chimera (PROTAC)-mediated21 knockdown of TDP-43 in mature neurons (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1a–d). TDP-43 is degraded by HaloPROTAC in a dose-dependent manner and in a process blocked by proteasome inhibition or the NEDD8 E1 inhibitor (Extended Data Fig. 1e–g). HaloTag-TDP-43 iPS cells were differentiated into mature excitatory cortical-like neurons (HaloTDP iNeurons) that expressed the layer V excitatory cortical marker CTIP2 and lacked expression of the inhibitory marker NKX2.1 or the neuronal progenitor marker PAX6 (Extended Data Fig. 1h). TDP-43 was also found to be correctly localized to the nucleus (Fig. 1b). Tagging of TDP-43 can alter its function and, whereas the HaloTag partially affected TDP-43 function (Extended Data Fig. 1i), UNC13A cryptic splicing and mRNA downregulation were robustly detected only on HaloPROTAC knockdown of TDP-43 (Fig. 1c,d and Extended Data Fig. 2a), similar to CRISPR interference (CRISPRi)-mediated knockdown (Extended Data Fig. 2b–f). Loss of UNC13A mRNA led to a time-dependent decrease in UNC13A protein whereby less than 5% of protein remained after 10 days of HaloPROTAC treatment (Fig. 1e,f). Immunofluorescence staining revealed a loss of synaptic UNC13A staining at synapsin-positive puncta (Fig. 1g,h). HaloPROTAC-mediated knockdown of TDP-43 in mature neurons did not lead to alterations in the RNA levels of N-methyl-d-aspartate and AMPA receptor subunits as assessed by reverse transcription–quantitative PCR (RT–qPCR) (Extended Data Fig. 2g).

a, Schematic of HaloTag insertion at the start of TARDBP exon 2 and genomic PCR (n = 1) confirming editing. b, Immunofluorescence showing nuclear TDP-43 localization in untreated (NT) HaloTDP iNeurons and loss following HaloPROTAC treatment (n = 3). c, RT–PCR analysis of UNC13A splicing following TDP-43 knockdown. d, Quantification of c; n = 12 biological replicates from 3 experiments. e, Western blot of HaloTDP iNeurons treated with 30 nM HaloPROTAC-E for the indicated times. f, Quantification of e; n = 2 biological replicates. g, Synapsin and UNC13A immunofluorescence in 4-week-old HaloTDP iNeurons cultured on rat astrocytes after 2 weeks of TDP-43 depletion. h, UNC13A intensity at synapsin-positive terminals (control n = 116; TDP-43 knockdown n = 115 synapses; 3 experiments). i, mEPSCs from control (n = 12) and UNC13A-knockdown (n = 13) iNeurons (3 experiments), with representative and mean traces, frequency and inter-event interval cumulative distributions. j, mEPSCs from control (n = 20) and TDP-43-knockdown (n = 22) HaloTDP iNeurons (3 experiments), with representative and mean traces, frequency and inter-event interval cumulative distributions. k, Representative MEA raster plots (60 s) for control (DIV38) and UNC13A-(DIV32) and TDP-43-(DIV38) knockdown; electrode bursts, blue; network bursts, pink. l,m, Network synchrony over time in control versus UNC13A- (l) or TDP-43- (m) knockdown iNeurons; knockdown values normalized to control (n = 18 wells, 3 experiments). Symbols indicate independent experiments. In l,m, lines connect parallel differentiations recorded on the same MEA plate. Statistics: two-sided Student’s t-test (d); Gaussian linear mixed-effects model (LMM) with two-sided Satterthwaite-corrected t-tests (h–j); two-sided ratio paired t-tests (l,m). *P < 0.05; **P < 0.01; ***P < 0.001; ****P < 0.0001. Uncropped gels are shown in Supplementary Fig. 1. Scale bars, 10 µm. In all figures, error bars represent mean ± s.e.m. CTRL, control; DIV, days in vitro; FC, fold change; KD, knockdown; NS, not significant; NT, no treatment; PSI, percentage spliced in.

Previous investigations of the physiological functions of UNC13A have been mainly conducted using primary rodent neurons with limited studies in human neurons18,19,20,22. We therefore sought to assess the impact of UNC13A loss in human iPS cell-derived neurons (Extended Data Fig. 2h). Whole-cell patch clamp recordings showed that depletion of UNC13A through CRISPRi impaired synaptic transmission, as evidenced by a reduction in the frequency of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) (Fig. 1i), consistent with a presynaptic deficit and in line with previously published work19,20. HaloPROTAC-mediated TDP-43 depletion also reduced mEPSC frequency (Fig. 1j), mirroring the presynaptic deficit observed on UNC13A loss. Treatment with 6-cyano-7-nitroquinoxaline-2,3-dione (CNQX) blocked mEPSCs, confirming that synaptic events were mediated primarily by means of fast AMPA receptor-mediated glutamatergic transmission (Extended Data Fig. 3a). Whereas UNC13A depletion had no effect on mEPSC amplitude, consistent with a purely presynaptic deficit (Extended Data Fig. 3b), TDP-43 depletion led to a modest reduction in amplitude (Extended Data Fig. 3c), suggesting extra postsynaptic deficits independent of UNC13A depletion. Passive membrane properties remained comparable between control and UNC13A–TDP-43 depleted neurons (Extended Data Fig. 3d,e).

To investigate the effect of UNC13A and TDP-43 loss on network activity, we carried out multi-electrode array (MEA) recordings. We found that either UNC13A or TDP-43 depletion induced a disordered and asynchronous pattern of network activity, measured by a reduction in the normalized electrode cross-correlations (Fig. 1k–m). This result indicates that UNC13A–TDP-43 depleted neurons fail to support network-level activity. The number of active electrodes remained consistent (Extended Data Fig. 3g) and phase-contrast images showed comparable cell coverage between conditions (Extended Data Fig. 3h), ruling out issues with electrode coverage as a confounding factor. CNQX treatment of control neurons confirmed network synchrony was highly dependent on fast AMPA receptor-mediated synaptic transmission (Extended Data Fig. 3f). Whereas extra MEA metrics were also affected by both TDP-43 and UNC13A loss, the network synchrony deficit was the largest and most consistently observed change (Extended Data Fig. 3g). Thus, we show that TDP-43 depletion substantially impairs fast glutamatergic synaptic transmission and synchronized network activity in human neurons, mirroring a comparable loss of synaptic function and network activity induced by direct UNC13A loss.

Knockdown of TDP-43 leads to cryptic exon inclusion within UNC13A intron 20 along with an independent downstream intron retention event at intron 31 and other lower-frequency splicing abnormalities throughout the UNC13A mRNA transcript6,7. To determine the degree to which protein loss is dependent on the UNC13A intron 20 cryptic exon, we performed CRISPR–Cas9 gene editing to remove the cryptic exon from the genome of SH-SY5Y cells (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). Using two single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs) we made a homozygous deletion of 233 nucleotides (nt) that contain both splice acceptors and the common donor splice site of the cryptic exon. In wild-type (WT) cells containing the full UNC13A gene there was robust induction of UNC13A mis-splicing after TDP-43 depletion as assessed by reverse transcription–PCR (RT–PCR) (Extended Data Fig. 4c,d), whereas in cells with genomic deletion of the UNC13A cryptic exon, no cryptic splicing was detected (Extended Data Fig. 4c,d). Cryptic exon deletion rescued correctly spliced levels of UNC13A mRNA, as determined by RT–qPCR, and led to roughly 75% rescue of UNC13A protein following TDP-43 knockdown (Extended Data Fig. 4e–g). We subsequently deleted the UNC13A cryptic exon in iPS cells (Extended Data Fig. 5a–e) and detected a similar rescue in UNC13A RNA and protein following CRISPRi-mediated knockdown of TDP-43, confirming the relevance of this event in iPS cell-derived neurons (Extended Data Fig. 5f–k). In the UNC13A cryptic exon deletion cell line, we performed further CRISPR–Cas12 gene editing to add a HaloTag in the TARDBP gene to efficiently induce TDP-43 loss after differentiation (Extended Data Fig. 6). Similar to results in SH-SY5Y cells, genomic deletion of the UNC13A cryptic exon in HaloTDP iNeurons rescued UNC13A splicing at the exon 20–21 junction and restored mRNA and presynaptic protein levels (Fig. 2a–h), demonstrating this splicing event is the main driver of TDP-43-dependent UNC13A loss.

TDP-43 knockdown yields synaptic transmission defects similar to those induced by direct depletion of UNC13A. However, TDP-43 has hundreds of validated RNA targets, regulating splicing, stability and transport of transcripts involved in virtually every aspect of neuronal function. Therefore, the reduction in synaptic transmission could reflect a multi-gene insult affecting pathways including synaptic vesicle trafficking, Ca2+ signalling and active zone organization. To determine the extent to which UNC13A cryptic exon inclusion contributes to impaired synaptic function following loss of TDP-43, we performed whole-cell patch clamping experiments in WT and cryptic exon deletion lines. Rescue of this single cryptic exon largely restored synaptic transmission following TDP-43 depletion with an 80% recovery in mEPSC frequency (Fig. 2i,j). mEPSC amplitude was still marginally (roughly 10%) reduced, supporting the conclusion that UNC13A cryptic exon deletion rescues specifically presynaptic function (Extended Data Fig. 7a). Passive membrane properties were similar between conditions (Extended Data Fig. 7b). As mEPSC frequency is influenced by synapse number, we measured excitatory synapse density along the dendrites of iNeurons. We found that TDP-43-knockdown neurons had fewer synapses than controls, a feature that persisted even when the UNC13A cryptic exon was deleted (Extended Data Fig. 7c,d), suggesting a strong recovery in synapse function in the remaining synapses.

Despite the small reduction in synapse number, MEA recordings showed that deletion of the UNC13A cryptic exon in TDP-43-depleted neurons restored synchronous network activity, indicating effective neurotransmitter release and propagation of signalling across the network (Fig. 2k,l and Extended Data Fig. 7e). This represented the most robustly rescued MEA metric (Extended Data Fig. 7f). Taken together, these findings show that correction of a single cryptic exon splicing event (intron 20 UNC13A cryptic exon) is sufficient to restore synaptic transmission and rescue the asynchronous patterns of network activity caused by TDP-43 loss. Active electrodes and cell coverage were comparable across conditions (Extended Data Fig. 7f,g). Likewise, analysis of neuronal survival confirmed that network-level changes were not attributable to changes in viability due to TDP-43 loss (Extended Data Fig. 7h) demonstrating that TDP-43 driven UNC13A loss drives a functional synaptic deficit in otherwise structurally intact, viable neurons.

The rescue of UNC13A levels and restoration of synaptic signalling conferred by deletion of the UNC13A cryptic exon in the context of TDP-43 knockdown highlights the therapeutic potential of targeting this event in patients. We therefore sought to identify ASOs that can induce splice switching similar to those successful in targeting splicing events in SMN2 and STMN2 (refs. 23,24). We first designed locked nucleic acid-modified ASOs that targeted regions covering the cryptic exon acceptor and donor splice sites (Extended Data Fig. 8a). We screened the ASOs by transfection in SK-N-BE(2) cells and assessed their ability to restore UNC13A splicing at the exon 20–21 junction by RT–PCR (Extended Data Fig. 8b) and found that 21-nt ASOs targeting the donor splice site could restore UNC13A splicing. We confirmed splicing rescue and ability to restore UNC13A RNA and UNC13A protein levels in SH-SY5Y cells (Extended Data Fig. 8c–g). To improve therapeutic tolerance, we adapted the best performing ASOs to have full 2′-O-methoxyethyl (MOE) ribose-modified bases and tested their ability to rescue UNC13A splicing and restore protein levels in HaloTDP iNeurons (Fig. 3a–c and Extended Data Fig. 8h). We found these could restore splicing to more than 90% and protein levels to 30–50% of normal levels. Treatment with the M21-4 MOE ASO led to increased presynaptic UNC13A protein expression at synapsin-positive puncta following TDP-43 depletion compared with treatment with the control scrambled ASO (Fig. 3d). To identify ASOs that could increase protein rescue above 50% of normal levels, we carried out a secondary screen by performing an ASO walk along the cryptic donor site with 18-nt MOE-based ASOs (Extended Data Fig. 9a). We evaluated the ability of the 18-nt ASOs to rescue splicing in SH-SY5Y cells by RT–PCR (Extended Data Fig. 9b) and confirmed that the best performing 18-nt ASOs could rescue correct UNC13A mRNA splicing to more than 90%, and protein to more than 50% in SH-SY5Y cells and HaloTDP iNeurons (Fig. 3e,f and Extended Data Fig. 9c–h). In addition, we performed amplicon sequencing, which confirmed the ability of ASOs to rescue both reference and risk alleles in our HaloTDP iNeurons (Extended Data Fig. 9i).

To validate the efficacy of UNC13A ASOs to rescue cryptic splicing in an in vivo model, we generated humanized UNC13A (hUNC13A) reporter mice, in which mouse intron 20 was replaced with human UNC13A intron 20 containing the cryptic exon. TDP-43 knockdown was performed by tail vein injection of an adeno-associated virus encoding a synthetic microRNA targeting the mouse Tardbp gene (Fig. 3g). On the same day, intracerebroventricular injections were performed in hUNC13A reporter mice with the M21-4 MOE ASO or artificial cerebrospinal fluid. Three weeks post-injection, spinal cords were dissected from the mice. RT–PCR analysis from spinal cord tissue following knockdown of TDP-43 showed no cryptic exon inclusion in WT mice and robust cryptic exon inclusion in hUNC13A reporter mice, which was partially rescued by administration of UNC13A splice-correcting ASO (Fig. 3h–k). Overall, these results show that ASOs can reduce inclusion of the UNC13A cryptic exon on TDP-43 knockdown both in vitro and in vivo, and can rescue UNC13A protein expression to above 50% in cultured neurons.

Unc13a heterozygous knockout mice and individuals with heterozygous LoF UNC13A mutations are viable and do not present with abnormal neurophysiology18,25. Recovery of UNC13A expression to WT levels after TDP-43 LoF is probably not required to restore synapse function, in agreement with previous work in primary mouse cultures that showed that clear deficits in synapse function are only observed when expression of Unc13a falls below 30% of normal physiological levels20,25. Indeed, treatment with M18-17 ASO, which rescues UNC13A levels to more than 50% of control, was able to rescue synaptic transmission as measured by an increase in mEPSC frequency (Fig. 4a). We then tested our M21-4 ASO, which rescues UNC13A protein levels to roughly 30% of normal levels. Despite the lower level of protein rescue, treatment with M21-4 ASO also rescued synaptic transmission following TDP-43 depletion as measured by an increase in mEPSC frequency (Fig. 4b). mEPSC amplitude and passive membrane properties were unaffected by treatment with ASOs (Extended Data Fig. 10a–d), suggesting that ASO treatment specifically rescues presynaptic deficits caused by the cryptic exon in UNC13A.
